newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr down and desperate after jobs blow.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr down and desperate after jobs blow.

text.p: The Australian dollar sank 1/4 cent to test the week's 18-month lows Thursday as desperately weak labour data made another rate cut seem inevitable.

The notoriously volatile employment measure lived up to its billing, rising just 11,900 in June when analysts had counted on a bounce of around 40,000 to correct the shock 40,300 drop seen in May. The breakdown was even worse with full-time jobs actually down by 16,900, which made a two month fall of 40,000.
Analysts were unanimous in labelling the data as dire and and in expecting another rate cut, although most thought the RBA would wait for inflation and wages data later this month.

By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the dollar was pondering a bleak future at US$0.7418/23 having reeled from US$0.7440/45 before the figures hit dealing screens. The dollar had finished at US$0.7435/40 Wednesday and under pressure as concerns about what the figures might say wore away an offshore rally to US$0.7493.

The worries were fully justified by the actual result with the meagre rise in jobs being beneath even the most bearish market forecast. Despite three official rate cuts in the second half of 1996 and another in May, the economy had actually lost a net 4,000 jobs in the first half of this year, while full-time employment was down a massive 63,900.

The one bright spot was a sizeable fall in the unemployment rate to 8.5 percent from 8.8 percent in May. But even this was tarnished as it came largely as a result of people ceasing to look for work, presumably because jobs were so hard to find.
The discouragement effect saw the participation rate -- the labour force expressed as a percentage of the population aged 15 and over -- fall to 63.0 from an already low 63.2.
This was its lowest level since October 1994 and analysts noted that if the rate had stayed at last year's average of 63.5, unemployment would have stood at 9.2 percent.
Since the Reserve Bank's charter expressely commits it to reducing unemployment, the money market concluded the bank would have no option but to ease policy to get growth gowing.

The 90-day bank bill future for September climbed seven basis points to a contract high of 94.97 as a result, almost entirely pricing in a 0.50 point cut in the present 5.50 percent official cash rate.

Bonds yields tumbled right along the curve and the 10-year bond dived 11 basis points to 6.62 percent, its lowest level since February 1994, taking the spread over 10-year U.S. Treasuries to just 37 basis points, a 16-year trough.
There was even a risk the RBA could ease as soon as Friday morning, although analysts felt the bank would not want to be seen responding to bad economic data.
That might smack of panic and prove counter productive for consumer sentiment, particularly if the media portrayed it as a move born of desperation.
Instead most thought the bank would wait for consumer price and wages data on July 23 and 24, which were expected to show inflation falling even further, and tag an easing to them.
If their calculation were correct and the bank cut by half a point it would take official rates below those in the U.S..
This would be an almost unprecedented event and dealers feared offshore investors would respond with their feet, as many have been doing since the last easing on May 23.

The dollar had been holding around 78 cents before that cut meaning its had fallen almost five percent since. It breached major technical levels in the process and chart watchers were looking for a retreat to 73 cents whether the bank eased or not.
The truly bearish noted that if the bank did move this month the market could well start to price in a sixth easing, a development which could see the dollar back at 70 cents by year end.
On the crosses the local currency slipped to 80.60/70 yen from 80.90/00 late here Wednesday and to 56.5 in trade weighted terms from 56.8.

Also out today were consumer credit figures for May which were actually quite firm but lost in the all the jobs noise. Lending rose 1.0 percent for the month, lifting annual growth to 10.1 percent from 9.5 percent in April and ending nine straight months of slowing growth.
Within that, lending for both housing and business rose 1.1 percent on the month while personal credit was up 0.6 percent.
